passages.t: Older men, older women, and younger women
passages.happening:
“But as for you, speak the things that are consistent with sound doctrine” (verse 1).

“Older men are to be temperate, dignified, self-controlled, and sound in faith, love, and perseverance. Older women, likewise, are to be reverent in their behavior, not slanderers or addicted to much wine, but teachers of good. In this way they can train the young women to love their husbands and children, to be self-controlled, pure, managers of their households, kind, and submissive to their own husbands, so that the word of God will not be discredited” (verses 2-5).
passages.hearers:
The false teachers of chapter 1 said they knew God, but their lives denied it. Now Paul shows what true teaching looks like in ordinary lives. ‘Sound doctrine’ means healthy teaching, and healthy teaching makes healthy people.

He goes through the church group by group, starting with the oldest. Older men are to be steady and serious, and ‘sound’, healthy, in faith, love and endurance. Older people were honoured in the ancient world, and Paul asks them to deserve it.

Older women are given real work: they are to be ‘teachers of good’. In a world where older women's influence was mostly inside the home, this was a true ministry. Paul warns them against two failings that writers of the time often joked about in older women, gossip and heavy drinking. He wants their words and their habits to be trustworthy, so that younger women can learn from them.

The list for younger women matched what respectable homes in the Roman world admired: love for husband and children, self-control, purity, care for the household, kindness, and submission to their own husbands.

Then comes the reason: ‘so that the word of God will not be discredited’. The church was new and suspected. Critics said the faith broke up families. Paul wanted Christian homes to show the opposite, so that outsiders would see something good and respect the message.

One word runs through this whole chapter: ‘self-controlled’. It is asked of older men, older women, younger women and younger men alike (verses 2, 5, 6). Everyone is called to the same steady mind.
passages.ot:
The Old Testament honours age: “You are to rise in the presence of the elderly, honor the aged, and fear your God” (Leviticus 19:32), and “Gray hair is a crown of glory; it is attained along the path of righteousness” (Proverbs 16:31).

It honours the teaching of older women too. Proverbs describes a woman of strength: “She opens her mouth with wisdom, and faithful instruction is on her tongue” (Proverbs 31:26). And the psalmist prays to keep teaching into old age: “Even when I am old and gray, do not forsake me, O God, until I proclaim Your power to the next generation” (Psalm 71:18).

Marriage goes back to the beginning: “For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and they will become one flesh” (Genesis 2:24).
passages.hard:
Does verse 5, ‘submissive to their own husbands’, ask wives to submit to their husbands today? What do Christians agree on, and where do they differ?

Much is agreed. Men and women are equally made in God's image and equally saved by grace. Paul asks every group in this chapter for the same self-control and goodness. He gives older women real teaching work. And his reason is the good name of the gospel.

Beyond that, Christians who share the same faith read this verse differently. It is a question that divides faithful churches, not the faith, and these notes do not choose.

Complementarians hold that men and women are equal in worth but given different callings in marriage, and that a wife's submission to her husband is a lasting pattern, not only a nod to Roman custom. They note that Paul elsewhere grounds the pattern in Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:22-33), that a husband's headship means self-giving love, not control, and that submission is a wife's own free response, never something a husband may demand or enforce.

Egalitarians hold that men and women are equal in worth and in calling. They read Paul here as applying the gospel inside the household customs of his day, and they point to the reason he gives: so that the word of God will not be discredited by outsiders who expected such behaviour. They note that Ephesians begins its household passage with ‘Submit to one another’ (Ephesians 5:21), that the same chapter's words to slaves are no longer read as approving slavery, and that where a partnership of equals no longer brings disgrace, the same concern for the gospel's good name points to marriages of mutual submission.

Nothing here licenses harshness or abuse. Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger. If you are in an abusive marriage, seek safety first. Talk to a pastor or a counselor you trust, or call a local domestic violence line. These notes are not legal advice.

If you are being hurt in some other place, at home, at work or in a church, the same is true. Tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Paul asks older believers to teach younger ones by word and by life. If you are older, ask who you could encourage or teach. If you are younger, ask who you could learn from. Ask whether your home shows outsiders something good about Christ. And ask whether your words are trustworthy, or whether gossip has crept in.

passages.t: Younger men, and Titus as an example
passages.happening:
“In the same way, urge the younger men to be self-controlled” (verse 6).

Then Paul speaks to Titus himself. “In everything, show yourself to be an example by doing good works. In your teaching show integrity, dignity, and wholesome speech that is above reproach, so that anyone who opposes us will be ashamed, having nothing bad to say about us” (verses 7-8).
passages.hearers:
For younger men, Paul names one thing: self-control. It is the same word he has used for everyone. Young men in every age are tempted to let their strength, anger or desires run them. Paul asks them to rule themselves.

Then he turns to Titus, who seems to have been young himself. Titus is not only to tell others how to live. He is to show them. ‘In everything, show yourself to be an example.’ People learn more from what they see than from what they hear.

His teaching must have ‘integrity’, meaning it is honest and not twisted for gain, unlike the teachers of chapter 1. It must have ‘dignity’, a seriousness that fits the message. And his speech must be ‘wholesome’, healthy, the same family of words as ‘sound’.

The reason is again the watching world: ‘so that anyone who opposes us will be ashamed, having nothing bad to say about us’. Paul does not ask Titus to win arguments. He asks him to live so well that accusations have nothing to stick to.
passages.ot:
Proverbs honours both young and old: “The glory of young men is their strength, and gray hair is the splendor of the old” (Proverbs 20:29). The psalmist asks how a young man can keep to the right road: “How can a young man keep his way pure? By guarding it according to Your word” (Psalm 119:9).

The young Samuel is the picture of a life that others could respect: “And the boy Samuel continued to grow in stature and in favor with the LORD and with man” (1 Samuel 2:26). And the Teacher says, “Remember your Creator in the days of your youth” (Ecclesiastes 12:1).
passages.asks: Paul asks young men for self-control and leaders for an example. Ask what in your life most needs ruling: anger, desire, words, or the wish to win. Ask whether the people who watch you see the gospel in what you do. And ask whether there is anything in your life an opponent could rightly point to.

passages.happening: “Slaves are to submit to their own masters in everything, to be well-pleasing, not argumentative, not stealing from them, but showing all good faith, so that in every respect they will adorn the teaching about God our Savior” (verses 9-10).
passages.hearers:
Slavery was everywhere in the Roman world, Crete included. Slaves worked in houses, fields, mines and workshops; some were trusted managers, others did crushing labour. People became slaves through war, through being born to an enslaved mother, through debt, or by being abandoned as babies and sold. Roman slavery was not based on race, and many slaves in the cities could hope to be freed one day. But by law a slave was property. A slave could be bought and sold, beaten, separated from family and used sexually by the master.

Many early Christians were slaves. Notice what these slaves heard when the letter was read. They were spoken to directly, as people who could choose how to live, not as tools. Pilfering from a master was a common complaint in ancient writing, and Paul asks for honesty. But then he says something remarkable. Slaves, people the world counted as property, could ‘adorn the teaching about God our Savior’. ‘Adorn’ means to make beautiful, like setting a jewel. The lowest people in the household were given the dignity of making the gospel shine.

Notice too that this letter says nothing here to masters. In Ephesians and Colossians Paul tells masters to give up threats and to remember that they too have a Master in heaven (Ephesians 6:9; Colossians 4:1).
passages.ot:
Israel's law set limits on slavery. It made kidnapping a person a capital crime: “Whoever kidnaps another man must be put to death, whether he sells him or the man is found in his possession” (Exodus 21:16). It said, “Do not return a slave to his master if he has taken refuge with you” (Deuteronomy 23:15). And a fellow Israelite sold into service was to go free: “in the seventh year you must set him free” (Deuteronomy 15:12).

Job says why he could not treat his servants as less than himself: “Did not He who made me in the womb also make them? Did not the same One form us in the womb?” (Job 31:15). And the God of Israel shows no favouritism: he is “the great, mighty, and awesome God, showing no partiality and accepting no bribe” (Deuteronomy 10:17).
passages.hard:
Why does Paul tell slaves to submit instead of condemning slavery? Paul does not command the end of slavery here, and that should not be softened. He writes to a small, powerless movement in an empire where slavery was everywhere and slave revolts were crushed with great violence.

But within that world he does what ordinary household rules did not. He speaks to slaves as people who answer to God and who can make the gospel beautiful. Elsewhere he tells masters to give up threats, and puts master and slave under one Lord, with no favouritism (Ephesians 6:9). On the most common reading of a debated verse, he tells slaves to gain their freedom if they can (1 Corinthians 7:21), and he asks Philemon to take back Onesimus “no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother” (Philemon 1:16). Many readers see in this the seeds of the truth that would undo slavery: every person bears God's image, and in Christ there is neither slave nor free (Galatians 3:28).

The history of verses like these is painful. In the Atlantic slave trade and in the American South, slaveholders and many preachers used them to demand obedience from enslaved Africans and to defend slavery as biblical, while they ignored the words to masters and the equality of all in Christ. That was a misuse, and it was wrong. Atlantic slavery, built on race and kidnapping, was very different from the Roman kind, and the law of Moses punished kidnapping with death. Christians who opposed slavery drew on the same Bible, on human dignity, the exodus and the gospel. The church's record was mixed, and it must be named honestly.

Nor are these verses a simple rule for employment today. A worker is not property, and a boss is not an owner. Some of what Paul says, to work honestly and with good faith, can be applied to work with care. But no one should use these verses to demand silence about mistreatment at work.

The Honest Answer ‘Why didn't the Bible just ban slavery?’ goes further.
passages.asks: Paul says that even people the world despised could make the gospel beautiful. Ask whom you treat as beneath you, and whether you see in them someone who might adorn the teaching about God. Ask whether your work, whatever it is, shows honesty and good faith. And if you have power over others, ask how you use it.

passages.t: The grace of God has appeared
passages.happening:
Now Paul gives the reason for everything in the chapter. “For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to everyone. It instructs us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live sensible, upright, and godly lives in the present age, as we await the blessed hope and glorious appearance of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ” (verses 11-13).

“He gave Himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for Himself a people for His own possession, zealous for good deeds” (verse 14).

“Speak these things as you encourage and rebuke with all authority. Let no one despise you” (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
‘For’ is the hinge. Why should old and young, men and women, slave and free live this way? Because God's grace has appeared.

Grace ‘appeared’ when Christ came into the world. And it brings salvation ‘to everyone’, every kind of person in Paul's list, including the slaves.

Then Paul says something surprising about grace. It ‘instructs us’. The word is the one used for bringing up a child, teaching and training. We usually think of grace as forgiveness, and it is. But in Titus, grace is also a teacher. It teaches us to say no to what is wrong and yes to a sensible, fair and godly life, right now, ‘in the present age’.

And we live that way while we wait. The Christian life sits between two appearings. Grace has appeared in Christ's first coming. We wait for ‘the glorious appearance’ of Christ when he returns. The Greek word gives English ‘epiphany’. It was used for a god showing himself or a ruler arriving in a city in splendour.

Who is coming? ‘Our great God and Savior Jesus Christ.’ And what did he do? He ‘gave Himself for us’. He set us free from lawlessness, cleaned us, and made us ‘a people for His own possession’, a phrase God first used of Israel at Sinai. And that people is ‘zealous for good deeds’: not saved by them, but eager to do them.

Verse 15 sends Titus back to work. He is to teach all this with authority, and not let anyone look down on him.
passages.ot:
‘His own possession’ is what God called Israel at Sinai: “you will be My treasured possession out of all the nations—for the whole earth is Mine” (Exodus 19:5).

Redeeming his people from wrongdoing is God's own promise in the psalms: “And He will redeem Israel from all iniquity” (Psalm 130:8). Ezekiel heard God promise the same: “I will save them from all their apostasies by which they sinned, and I will cleanse them. Then they will be My people, and I will be their God” (Ezekiel 37:23).

And Isaiah gave the coming child the name “Mighty God” (Isaiah 9:6).
passages.hard:
‘Our great God and Savior Jesus Christ.’ Is Paul calling Jesus God?

Most translations, the BSB among them, and most readers take this phrase as speaking of one person: Jesus Christ is our great God and Savior. With the church in every age, these notes confess that Jesus Christ is truly God and truly man, one with the Father, the Son through whom we are saved. That confession does not rest on this verse alone. John opens his Gospel with “the Word was God” (John 1:1), Thomas says to the risen Jesus, “My Lord and my God!” (John 20:28), and Hebrews says of the Son, “Your throne, O God, endures forever and ever” (Hebrews 1:8).

Notice how naturally the letter does this. Paul calls God ‘Savior’ (1:3; 2:10; 3:4) and Jesus Christ ‘Savior’ (1:4; 2:13; 3:6), often side by side. Saving is God's own work, and Jesus does it.

And notice what the verse is for. It is not given to win an argument. It is given to people waiting in hope, so that they know who is coming: not a stranger, but the God who ‘gave Himself for us’.
passages.asks: Paul says that grace is a teacher. Ask what grace is teaching you to say no to, and what it is teaching you to say yes to. Ask whether you are waiting for Christ's appearing with hope. And ask whether you are ‘zealous for good deeds’, not to earn anything, but because you have already been given everything.
